content:
Hi folks,

Probably a noob question here: when I checkout to an old commit hash in Mathlib (let's say, before a PR) and then apply the diff from the PR and run lake build again, it seems to be extremely slow and can take more than an hour. The time needed is longer when the PR edits a file early in the dependency chain so a lot of files need to be built again. Is this normal? What is the common workflow here in a dev environment to check that the code actually works with the rest of Mathlib properly?

Thanks!
Did you lake exe cache get?
yes - but the cache is invalidated if I touch a file early in the dependency chain, right?
Yeah, but I still don't understand the issue you described

for example, if I start from an old commit and edit the file /Mathlib/Logic/Function/Basic.lean with a simple

diff --git a/Mathlib/Logic/Function/Basic.lean b/Mathlib/Logic/Function/Basic.lean
index a568026c238..b7f13b21865 100644
--- a/Mathlib/Logic/Function/Basic.lean
+++ b/Mathlib/Logic/Function/Basic.lean
@@ -654,6 +654,10 @@ lemma FactorsThrough.extend_comp {g : α → γ} (e' : β → γ) (hf : FactorsT
     extend f g e' ∘ f = g :=
   funext fun a => hf.extend_apply e' a

+@[simp]
+lemma extend_const (f : α → β) (c : γ) : extend f (fun _ ↦ c) (fun _ ↦ c) = fun _ ↦ c :=
+  funext fun _ ↦ ite_id _
+
 @[simp]
 theorem extend_comp (hf : Injective f) (g : α → γ) (e' : β → γ) : extend f g e' ∘ f = g :=
   funext fun a ↦ hf.extend_apply g e' a

then when I run lake build, I get

+ lake build
✔ [567/5076] Built Mathlib.Logic.Function.Basic
✔ [568/5076] Built Mathlib.Logic.Function.Conjugate
✔ [569/5076] Built Mathlib.Algebra.CharZero.Defs
✔ [570/5076] Built Mathlib.Data.FunLike.Basic
✔ [571/5076] Built Mathlib.Logic.IsEmpty
✔ [572/5076] Built Mathlib.Data.Subtype
...

which takes extremely long.

how can I reasonably work on this file while making sure that my changes are compatible with rest of mathlib and won't break lake build? Of course one way is to use the lean server and see that my file compiles (or running lake build filename.lean) but is that enough to verify that my code will be compatible with rest of lean (e.g. I can mess up a definition and file will compile on its own but all of mathlib won't compile, right?)

If you make a change that might affect all of the files downstream—note that e.g. @[simp] is picked up by every subsequent invocation of simp, which may now do more simplification or even break if the new lemma doesn’t fit well into the simp set—you do simply need to build all the downstream files to find out how they are affected. :) (This is one of the tradeoffs of having arbitrarily complex elaboration.)

The typical workflow for me when adjusting something early in the hierarchy is pushing to a PR (possibly a draft PR) and letting CI build it while I do something else, then using lake exe cache get or just inspecting the logs when CI is finished.
(Of course, usually I have another file open that’s not too far downstream to spot check the effects of the file I’m changing, but this doesn’t ensure anything.)

Thanks so much for the answer! How long does this usually take?

It would be very ideal if we could reduce this to <1-3 minutes (under no computational constraints)

Mert Ünsal said:

Thanks so much for the answer! How long does this usually take?

This very much depends on how many cores you have and how fast they are!

For a "normal" machine a build time of up to an hour sounds normal. For a modern fast machine with many cores you can get it down to about ten minutes.

I can run on very large number of cores with a lot of RAM (>32-64 GB) - is the speedup automatic with more cores or does it require setting some additional parameters.

P.S. if there are additional speed benefits I could probably go even higher

More cores doesn't give you more speed-up unfortunately, if you have a large amount of cores then the bottleneck is the "longest pole" in mathlib, the longest sequence of files each of which imports the one before, and it would not surprise me at all if Logic.Function.Basic were involved in that sequence given that it is right at the root of the tree.

Mathlib recently moved to a "module" system and there is a chance that this might help in the long run, but my understanding is that we are not quite ready here, and to be honest I think that adding a simp lemma might well be beyond what the module system can mitigate for because you've just changed the behaviour of the fundamental simp tactic in many thousands of files, all of which will need to be recompiled as a consequence.

Note that if you don't fancy spending your own electricity then you can make your change, push to a branch on your github fork of mathlib and let github compile for you, and then use lake exe cache get to get the precompiled oleans for your branch.

That makes sense. The goal here is really to have a fast verification cycle.

Practically can we find circumstances under which we don’t need to run the
whole tree? If I add a new theorem, or refactor a proof, or just fill a
sorry, an entire recompilation should not be needed, right? A friend of
mine told me that sometimes proofs can change types which I didn’t know
about, so not sure how that would work.

Mert Ünsal said:

refactor a proof, or just fill a sorry, an entire recompilation should not be needed, right?

Indeed, see the GIF here: #Lean Releases > releases of v4.24.0 through v4.29.0-rc1 @ 💬

I think adding a theorem still requires recompilation, since Lean has to check for name conflicts further down the line.
Oh actually if you make your theorem sorry-free, I think it'll also rebuild, because you changed the axioms that the theorem depends on.

Right -- the reason the gif is fast is because all that changed was the proof of a theorem, and this affects nothing downstream. The change above changes the behaviour of a tactic so recompiling is surely inevitable.

Thanks for the comments - in my setup I am unable to get the ~10 minute mentioned by @Kevin Buzzard, even with a lot of powerful CPU cores. Is there a setting that can help here to utilize more cores? How does the CI image run lake build?
To clarify, @Mert Ünsal, you are interested in running a lake build with no cached oleans, is that right? Perhaps post what hardware you have, and exactly how long it takes?

To resurrect this : I recently ran time lake build on a cleanly cloned mathlib with a Mac Studio M1 ultra with 64gb RAM, with the following output :

lake build 28117.20s user 11281.12s system 1883% cpu 34:51.54 total

If a build time of 10 minutes on a modern fast machine is possible, I would expect that mine would be more competitive than that. I would like to understand what makes it possible as well!
I don't know what machines are behind the !radar builds in mathlib CI but they are certainly only taking 10-15 minutes to build mathlib. Maybe @Joscha Mennicken can tell us more about those machines?

Peter Nelson said:

To resurrect this : I recently ran time lake build on a cleanly cloned mathlib with a Mac Studio M1 ultra with 64gb RAM, with the following output :

lake build 28117.20s user 11281.12s system 1883% cpu 34:51.54 total

If a build time of 10 minutes on a modern fast machine is possible, I would expect that mine would be more competitive than that. I would like to understand what makes it possible as well!

I don't think this is unexpected. The 10 minute build times are on 96 core machines.
Yeah, radar mathlib builds run on an AMD EPYC 9455 with 48 cores/96 threads and 125 GiB of memory
